Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
In message <a23a105e.04031...@posting.google.com>,
dan...@eposta.hu (Daneel) mumbled something about:

>Please refrain from namecalling, arguing for arguing's sake and other
>immature behaviour. Let's focus on the game we all love instead of
>trying to use the newsgroup as a means to bully, aggravate or
>discredit other people.

So Vermillian shouldn't have posted his spoilers, because he knew it
would aggravate a bunch of people. Right?

As someone else noted, welcome to the Internet. I'm hardly the only
person who wades in and says what he thinks; it's been around for a long
time. Look at Stefan, for example; he's in there slugging it out with
me toe-to-toe, and yet wants to take the "oh, i am a model of reasoned
discourse" position? Please. Five minutes for fighting, both of us.

However, I'm going to point out that the Internet also makes it possible
for one side of a discussion to be deliberately ignorant. There's no
tone of voice, there's no facial expressions, and most importantly, it's
much more difficult to carry on a debate... because you can't
immediately clarify your points when someone misreads or misunderstands
them, and you can always just snip out the parts you didn't agree with.

Over the past six years, I've found that certain people consistently are
not capable of reading English. This isn't a slam at Europeans, because
most of the people I refer to are native English speakers. But they
simply can't read what's being said, and can't understand it. I don't
know if it's a flaw in the much-maligned American educational system, or
what, but you can say "X is true", and someone will say "no, Y is
false!" I've brought this up before; it's an example of the "My dog has
four legs, all cats have four legs, my cat is a dog" chain of logic...
and you see it a LOT here.

This leads to irritation on everyone's part, and where in a face-to-face
discussion this would only lead to a raised voice and a cessation of all
other topics until the X/Y issue was resolved, the Internet doesn't have
a natural outflow for this. Someone is free to write on and on, drawing
elaborate conclusions from "Y is false!", whether or not Y had anything
to do with the topic at hand... and further disrupting and confusing the
discussion. I've also noticed that if you try to say "Y isn't relevant
to the issue", the person will immediately respond with an entire post
explaining why Y is false, completely derailing the topic. Good luck
trying to recover.

The only EFFECTIVE solution is not to try to debate anything over the
Internet. That won't happen and isn't a realistic solution, so as an
alternative to raised voices, you end up with people punctuating with
insults. Some people are relatively calm, but you may notice they also
back out of discussions as soon as the "Y is false" problem comes up;
they're taking the second approach, which is to not even bother trying
to convince people who aren't willing to listen. I'm not sure I agree
with that approach; not the sort of person to give up easily, you know.
But it does improve the signal-to-noise ratio, at the cost of allowing
incorrect information to be disseminated.

Which is worth more to you?

-- Derek

of how to behave on the internet, and I tend to see just as much flaming
(and certainly more totally random, irrelevant flaming, as opposed to
flaming that comes out of a particularly heated discussion of something
valid, like we tend to here). Usent flaming tends to revolve around:

<long discussion of mostly salient points, followed by>

"...see, you clearly don't understand, 'cause you are an idiot!"

<at which point madness ensues>

as opposed to web based BBS flame wars the generally tend to revolve around:

<short, badly spelled idiotic ramble with very limited grammar, followed by>

"you're MaMa! ASSSSSSSSSSSSSS!"

I spent a lot of time recently on the Heroclix BBS, which is a wasteland of
idiocy, flaming, and dumbness, for the most part (although I did learn to
appreciate Andrew as an ally :-), moderators or no.

Suffice to say, usenet strikes me as a oasis of good manners and intelligent
discussion compared to most of the web based BBS's I've been on (with the
SFB BBS a notable exception, probably due to the iron fist of the moderators
and the "old school" attitudes of most of the contributors).

Messages.Author: Alex Broadhead
Messages.Body:
Howdy,

Warning, there's an awful high context-to-commentary ratio in this
post, but it seemed important to leave most of it in...

> >Please refrain from namecalling, arguing for arguing's sake and other
> >immature behaviour. Let's focus on the game we all love instead of
> >trying to use the newsgroup as a means to bully, aggravate or
> >discredit other people.
>
> So Vermillian shouldn't have posted his spoilers, because he knew it
> would aggravate a bunch of people. Right?
>

> As someone else noted, welcome to the Internet. I'm hardly the only
> person who wades in and says what he thinks; it's been around for a long

> time. Look at Stefan, for example; he's in there slugging it out with
> me toe-to-toe, and yet wants to take the "oh, i am a model of reasoned
> discourse" position? Please. Five minutes for fighting, both of us.

Heh. Good analogy - as with hockey, on Usenet, the fights are often
at least as entertaining as the game...

> However, I'm going to point out that the Internet also makes it possible
> for one side of a discussion to be deliberately ignorant. There's no
> tone of voice, there's no facial expressions, and most importantly, it's
> much more difficult to carry on a debate... because you can't
> immediately clarify your points when someone misreads or misunderstands
> them, and you can always just snip out the parts you didn't agree with.

I'm not sure how much I agree with this. Firstly, there's an awful
lot of non-Usenet 'discussion' that seems to me to exhibit the same
'deliberate ignorance' property. In fact, as far as I can tell,
formal debate is more or less based entirely on selective exploitation
of that property, to say nothing of presidential 'debate'. And
secondly, I often find myself in face-to-face discussion wishing I had
everything written down and threaded, so that I could track the
development (and possible circularity) of argument, and make sure that
all the various important parts get addressed before I forget them,
etc. (Which provides a sort of 'artificial immediacy' to each branch
of the argument, if you follow me.) Finally, the lack of actual
immediacy can also be a blessing - in that one can (theoretically, I
know) think before one speaks, reread others' and one's own writing.

Of course, I'm not a very good extemporaenous face-to-face arguer.
Physical clues don't really help me a lot over (and I can't believe
I'm saying this) the accursed smileys. Any emotional heat
face-to-face is really going to make it difficult for me to proceed.
So I'm fairly biased here, but still I think there's a lot of plus to
go with the minus.

> Over the past six years, I've found that certain people consistently are
> not capable of reading English. This isn't a slam at Europeans, because
> most of the people I refer to are native English speakers. But they
> simply can't read what's being said, and can't understand it. I don't
> know if it's a flaw in the much-maligned American educational system, or
> what, but you can say "X is true", and someone will say "no, Y is
> false!" I've brought this up before; it's an example of the "My dog has
> four legs, all cats have four legs, my cat is a dog" chain of logic...
> and you see it a LOT here.

This looks like two different things to me. First there's 'deliberate
ignorance' or 'disunderstanding' as like to phrase it. This isn't a
case of not being able to understand, so much as willingly
misrepresenting the opposing facts or argument. This, while annoying
and despicable, is a tried and true debate tactic.

The other problem, which is not quite the same, is the inability to
parse or form a logical argument. This is not deliberate ignorance so
much as cluelessness, though at some point you do have to wonder how
it is that a human of a certain age has managed to avoid learning such
a basic thing. It's usually actually pretty easy to tell the two
apart, I think? And while there's not much you can do about the
former, other than to point out their fallacies, the latter should be
susceptible to education if you're patient. Heh.

> This leads to irritation on everyone's part, and where in a face-to-face
> discussion this would only lead to a raised voice and a cessation of all
> other topics until the X/Y issue was resolved, the Internet doesn't have
> a natural outflow for this. Someone is free to write on and on, drawing
> elaborate conclusions from "Y is false!", whether or not Y had anything
> to do with the topic at hand... and further disrupting and confusing the
> discussion. I've also noticed that if you try to say "Y isn't relevant
> to the issue", the person will immediately respond with an entire post
> explaining why Y is false, completely derailing the topic. Good luck
> trying to recover.
>
> The only EFFECTIVE solution is not to try to debate anything over the
> Internet. That won't happen and isn't a realistic solution, so as an
> alternative to raised voices, you end up with people punctuating with
> insults. Some people are relatively calm, but you may notice they also
> back out of discussions as soon as the "Y is false" problem comes up;
> they're taking the second approach, which is to not even bother trying
> to convince people who aren't willing to listen. I'm not sure I agree
> with that approach; not the sort of person to give up easily, you know.
> But it does improve the signal-to-noise ratio, at the cost of allowing
> incorrect information to be disseminated.
>
> Which is worth more to you?

I guess I fall into the former camp? I've thought about adopting the
alias or signature 'threadcutter', as my messages are so often the
leaves or 'twigs' (once removed from leaves) of message trees.

I can sort of see where you're coming from with the 'don't want to
leave the id10t looking like he was right' argument. But I think
there may be a fallacy there. If those following the discussion can
parse the arguments and evaluate the truth value of the premises, then
what is to be gained by following down the 'Y is false' branch?
Everyone who was interested in X has stopped paying attention. And if
those following the discussion _cannot_ parse the arguments and
evaluate the truth value of the premises, is a non-sequitur argument
('Y is false', 'X is true', 'Y is FALSE!', 'X is TRUE you freakin'
id10t!') likely to clear things up for them?

Further, I'm not sure that this really describes the problem that
Daneel was (beautifully naively) addressing (in the post quoted up
top). It seems to me that the source of most of the flameage is the
(sometimes accidental, but see the previous discussion of
'disunderstanding') descent of argument into ad hominem. (OK, so
sometimes there's not so much a descent as a plunge - many people seem
to have the mistaken impression that any reply by Derek in particular
is necessarily a challenge.) And the problem, as I see it, with being
to itchy on the trigger there is that you may mistake the clueless for
the deliberately ignorant, which is almost certainly not going to lead
to enlightenment...

OK, that was way too long to essentially just be a plea for patience
and giving people the benefit of the doubt until they're proven to be
Andrew. <insert smiley thing here>

On the other hand, I really enjoy watching the fights (from a safe
distance).

Hope that helps,
the _other_ Alex
